questions.question: What makes a web page responsive?
questions.title: Responsive web design foundations
questions.direct_answer: A responsive page adapts its layout, content, media, controls, and typography to the available environment instead of targeting one fixed screen. It starts with flexible normal flow, relative or constrained sizing, flexible images, and content-led layout; media or container queries add changes only when the design actually needs them.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner treats responsiveness as continuous adaptation rather than two device layouts.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Choosing breakpoints from popular device widths or hiding essential content on small screens.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Include zoom, user preferences, container context, and intermediate-width testing.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Responsive design serves a range of environments, not named devices.
Normal flow and flexible layout are the starting point.
Media and container queries handle meaningful layout changes.
Content, controls, images, and text must all remain usable.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Responsive design means a page remains understandable and usable across different available widths, zoom levels, orientations, input methods, and user preferences. It is broader than shrinking a desktop layout to fit a phone.

The starting point is the web's flexible normal flow. Blocks use available inline space, text wraps, and modern Flexbox or Grid layouts can distribute content without fixed coordinates. max-width constraints keep lines readable while percentages and flexible tracks let components contract.

Media queries introduce a change when the current arrangement stops working. Container queries can respond to a component's own available space, which is useful when the same card appears in a wide main area and a narrow sidebar.

For example, an article list can use one fluid column by default, become a multi-column Grid when each card can still retain a useful minimum width, and serve appropriately sized images through srcset. Controls keep readable labels and usable targets at every size.

The boundary is content and accessibility. Hiding essential information on small screens is not a responsive solution, and disabling zoom harms users. I test narrow and wide sizes, intermediate widths, text zoom, keyboard focus, long content, and both portrait and landscape instead of checking only two device presets. Performance is part of that experience. Responsive images and restrained asset loading keep a narrow device from receiving desktop-sized resources merely because the layout can visually squeeze them into place.

sections.title: Adapt relationships, not just dimensions
sections.content: A responsive design preserves content priority and task flow while presentation changes. Flexible defaults handle continuous variation; queries handle the points where a relationship genuinely needs a different arrangement.

sections.title: Breakpoints belong to the content
sections.content: A breakpoint is justified when navigation wraps badly, a text line becomes unreadable, or two regions no longer have enough usable space. Device names age quickly and do not describe split-screen windows, zoom, embedded components, or new hardware. Test the layout until it fails, then place the condition around that failure.

sections.title: Responsive decision
sections.content:
Flexible normal flow
  -> constrain readable measures and flexible media
  -> resize until a relationship fails
  -> add a media or container query for that relationship
  -> retest zoom, content, input, and intermediate widths

sections.title: Let a component respond to its container

questions.question: How do mobile-first media queries work?
questions.title: Mobile-first media queries
questions.direct_answer: Mobile-first CSS places the simplest narrow layout in the base rules, then uses min-width media queries to enhance the layout when more space is available. The approach reduces overrides and keeps unsupported queries on a usable baseline. Breakpoints should be chosen where content needs a new arrangement, not from device brand widths.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands mobile-first as progressive CSS and can explain the cascade.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Leaving the base incomplete or choosing min-width breakpoints from device labels.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate width queries from input and preference queries.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Base styles serve the narrow layout without a query.
min-width queries add enhancements as space increases.
Later rules need the same or appropriate specificity to override.
Choose breakpoints from content failure, not device names.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Mobile-first CSS begins with the layout that works in the most constrained width and places it outside media queries. Wider arrangements are enhancements inside min-width conditions.

For example, a profile page can stack its photo and details by default. At the width where both have enough room, a min-width query changes the component to two columns. A later query may widen the navigation, but each step preserves the earlier usable baseline.

The cascade still applies. A media query does not make a selector stronger, so source order, specificity, and cascade layers determine whether an enhancement overrides the base declaration.

Mobile-first does not mean designing only for phones or putting every property in a query. It describes the direction of progressive layout changes, while input capabilities and user preferences may need feature queries such as hover, pointer, prefers-reduced-motion, or prefers-color-scheme.

The boundary is content. If the wide layout is actually simpler for a particular component, forcing an ideology can create needless overrides. The goal is a clear baseline and justified enhancements, not a required count of min-width rules.

sections.title: Baseline first, enhancements upward
sections.content: The base rule answers what always works. Each min-width block then answers what becomes possible with more room. Reading the stylesheet from top to bottom follows the same direction as the layout gaining capability.

sections.title: Queries participate in the cascade
sections.content: Conditions decide whether declarations are eligible; they do not bypass normal CSS conflict resolution. Keep selectors intentionally similar and place broader enhancements in a predictable order. Range syntax and custom properties can improve readability, but they do not replace testing around the exact content transition.

sections.title: Progressive layout states
sections.content:
Base: one column, full-width actions
min-width: 40rem -> two content columns
min-width: 64rem -> persistent secondary navigation
Each state inherits the usable rules before it.

sections.title: Enhance a stacked card when space permits

questions.question: What does the viewport meta tag do on mobile browsers?
questions.title: Viewport meta tag on mobile
questions.direct_answer: The viewport meta tag tells mobile browsers how the layout viewport should relate to the device. width=device-width makes CSS pixels follow the device's available width, and initial-scale=1 starts at a 1:1 zoom level. Without it, a browser may use a wider legacy layout viewport and scale the page down, preventing narrow-layout queries from behaving as intended.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner knows why mobile browsers need viewport configuration.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Claiming the tag creates responsiveness or disabling zoom to stabilize the page.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish CSS pixels, device pixels, layout configuration, and actual responsive CSS.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: width=device-width matches the layout viewport to device width.
initial-scale=1 sets the initial zoom scale.
Without the tag, mobile browsers may emulate a wide desktop viewport.
Do not disable user zoom with maximum-scale or user-scalable=no.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Mobile browsers historically used a wide virtual layout viewport for desktop-only sites and then scaled the rendered page down. That made an old fixed-width page visible, but text appeared tiny and CSS saw a width much larger than the physical screen.

The viewport meta tag lets the document choose modern behaviour. width=device-width asks the layout viewport to match the device's available width in CSS pixels, while initial-scale=1 establishes the initial zoom level.

For example, a max-width: 30rem or narrow-screen media query can only describe the intended phone layout when the browser reports the appropriate viewport. Without the tag, the browser may keep evaluating a desktop-sized layout and simply show it zoomed out.

The tag does not make fixed layouts responsive by itself. Widths, media, typography, and controls still need flexible rules, and the page must be tested when zoomed.

The accessibility boundary is zoom control. maximum-scale=1 or user-scalable=no can prevent users from enlarging content and should not be used to hide layout problems. Responsive CSS should accommodate zoom instead of forbidding it.

sections.title: Configure the measuring surface
sections.content: Media queries and percentage layouts use the layout viewport as their reference. The meta tag makes that reference represent the mobile device rather than a legacy desktop canvas. It is configuration, not a layout technique.

sections.title: CSS pixels are not hardware pixels
sections.content: device-width is expressed in CSS pixels, which provide a stable coordinate system across device pixel densities. High-density screens may use several hardware pixels for one CSS pixel. Responsive design works with the CSS viewport while image selection can also consider pixel density.

sections.title: Mobile rendering with and without viewport configuration
sections.content:
| State | Layout viewport | Visible result |
|---|---|---|
| No viewport tag | Often legacy desktop width | Desktop layout scaled down |
| width=device-width | Device-width CSS viewport | Narrow responsive layout can activate |

sections.title: Use the standard accessible viewport declaration
sections.content:
```html Responsive page

Readable at the device width

``` The declaration configures the layout viewport without taking away the user's ability to zoom.

questions.question: How do srcset, sizes, and picture make images responsive?
questions.title: Responsive images with srcset, sizes, and picture
questions.direct_answer: srcset gives the browser image candidates and their widths or pixel densities; sizes describes the rendered image slot so the browser can choose an efficient candidate. picture lets the author switch sources for art direction or formats, while its img child provides the image, accessible text, and fallback. Width and height attributes reserve aspect-ratio space.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner distinguishes resolution switching, slot sizing, and art direction.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing width candidates without an accurate sizes value or omitting the img fallback.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect intrinsic dimensions to layout stability and preserve meaning across crops.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: srcset lists candidate image resources.
sizes describes the expected slot width for width-descriptor candidates.
picture selects sources for art direction or formats.
The img element remains required and owns alt text.
width and height reserve space and reduce layout shift.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Responsive images solve resolution, performance, and sometimes composition. With width descriptors, srcset lists each file's intrinsic width, such as 480w or 960w. sizes tells the browser how wide the image's rendered slot will be under relevant conditions.

The browser combines that slot estimate with device pixel density and other factors to choose a candidate before the CSS layout and all resources finish. The author does not command one exact file for every device; the browser selects from valid options.

picture serves a different need. Its source elements can provide a cropped composition at a condition or offer formats by type. The required img child remains the actual image element, supplies alt text and dimensions, and acts as the fallback when no source matches.

For example, a card image that fills the viewport on narrow pages but occupies half of a 60rem content area can declare sizes='(min-width: 60rem) 30rem, 100vw'. The browser can then avoid downloading a full desktop image for a small slot.

Width and height attributes should describe the source aspect ratio so space is reserved before loading and layout shift is reduced. The boundary is meaning: decorative images use empty alt text, while an art-directed crop must preserve the information described by the same accessible alternative. I verify the network choice in browser Developer Tools at several viewport widths and densities. An inaccurate sizes value can make valid markup repeatedly download a candidate much larger than the rendered slot needs.

sections.title: Candidates, slot, selection
sections.content: srcset answers which files exist. sizes estimates the slot they must fill. The browser chooses a suitable candidate. picture changes which source set is eligible when composition or file format must change.

sections.title: Resolution switching is not art direction
sections.content: Several resolutions of the same composition belong in one img srcset. A wide landscape hero and a tight portrait crop express different compositions, so picture source elements are appropriate. CSS background images require different techniques and do not carry img semantics or alt text.

sections.title: Browser image selection
sections.content:
Evaluate picture source media/type
  -> read srcset candidates
  -> evaluate sizes slot width
  -> combine slot with pixel density
  -> fetch a suitable resource
  -> render in reserved aspect-ratio space

sections.title: Provide art direction and resolution choices
sections.content: ```html ``` Narrow screens receive a tighter crop; each eligible source still offers an efficient resolution choice.

questions.question: When should CSS use px, rem, em, percentages, viewport units, or container units?
questions.title: Choosing CSS length units
questions.direct_answer: Use px for small fixed visual details, rem for sizes tied to the root text scale, em for values that should follow a component's local font size, percentages for a containing block relationship, viewport units for viewport-relative effects, and container query units for component-relative effects. Prefer constraints such as min(), max(), and clamp() over one unit everywhere.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner chooses units from the relationship a value should follow.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Declaring one universal best unit or using viewport units for body text without limits.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention reference pixels, container units, property-specific percentages, and bounded fluid values.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: rem follows the root font size; em follows the current element's font context.
Percentages resolve against a property-specific containing reference.
Viewport and container units follow different available regions.
px is a CSS reference pixel, not necessarily one hardware pixel.
Combine units with constraints instead of choosing one universal unit.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
CSS units express different relationships. px is a CSS reference pixel and works well for thin borders, icons, or details that need a stable visual size. It is not guaranteed to equal one physical screen pixel.

rem is relative to the root element's font size, so it is useful for typography and spacing that should follow the user's base text scale. em is relative to the relevant element's font context, which makes it useful when a component's padding or icon should scale with that component's text.

Percentages are relative to a containing reference defined by the property, so 50% width and 50% padding do not always answer the same geometric question. Viewport units follow the viewport; modern small, large, and dynamic viewport variants help with mobile browser interfaces.

Container query units such as cqi follow a query container's inline size. For example, a reusable card can use clamp with rem and cqi so its heading responds to the card's allocated width rather than the whole window.

I avoid sizing body text with viewport units alone because it can become too small or grow excessively and may respond poorly to zoom. The boundary is readability: min(), max(), and clamp() can combine a flexible relationship with accessible lower and upper limits. No single unit is correct for every property. Unit choice should also be consistent within a design token. A spacing scale based on rem is easier to reason about than unrelated conversions scattered through individual components.

sections.title: Every unit names a reference
sections.content: The useful question is not which unit is best, but what this value should respond to: a stable CSS reference, root text preference, local component text, containing block, viewport, or component container. That reference determines the unit.

sections.title: Relative values still need limits
sections.content: Fluid values are most reliable when bounded. clamp(1rem, 0.9rem + 0.5vw, 1.4rem) preserves a minimum and maximum while allowing gradual change. Container units improve component isolation, but they require an established query container and should still respect content and zoom testing.

sections.title: Unit and reference relationship
sections.content:
| Unit | Main reference | Good fit |
|---|---|---|
| px | CSS reference pixel | Border or small fixed detail |
| rem | Root font size | Type and shared spacing scale |
| em | Local font size | Component-relative padding |
| % | Property-specific containing reference | Flexible track or box |
| vw / dvh | Viewport | Viewport-relative region |
| cqi | Query container inline size | Reusable component fluidity |

sections.title: Combine readable limits with a fluid middle
